extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature, philosophy, and the theory of humor
extracted.subtask_description: An analytic, philosophical account of what makes things comic (the nature of the laughable), describing types of comic effect, their psychological/logic mechanisms, and social functions, illustrated with literary examples (Don Quixote, Moliere, Mark Twain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer of professional mannerisms to everyday life
rubrics_metrics.description: The ludicrous that results when a professional strategy or habit is applied to ordinary affairs of life, making people 'incapable of talking like ordinary people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually coarse, but can be refined when it also reveals a peculiarity of character; examples: Regnard's Joueur (gambling terms applied to persons) and Moliere's Femmes savantes (scientific ideas translated into feminine sensibility: 'Epicure me plait...', 'J'aime les tourbillons').

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast between particular (professional) logic and universal logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic effects arise from the contrast between a logic valid within a particular circle (professional logic) and universal/common-sense logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain customary ways of reasoning are true within some circles but absurd to the general public; the clash of these two logics produces special comic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic absurdity as a definite, particular kind
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurdity in the comic is not absurdity in general but a definite kind that reflects the special nature of its cause; it is an effect infused with the essence of the comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theories that reduce all comic to 'absurdity' miss that comic absurdity is a special inversion of common sense tied to particular causes (rigidity, automatism); making up effects from a generic definition of absurdity will often fail to produce laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion of common sense (privileged recollection dominating perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeing what one is thinking of instead of thinking of what one sees; a privileged recollection (idea) takes command of perception and moulds objects to itself (Don Quixote sees giants where others see windmills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common sense normally adapts ideas to objects; comic inversion makes ideas adapt objects to themselves, producing delusion carried out with logical precision (as in Don Quixote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity/automatism/obstinacy of mind (following one idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic characters err through obstinacy, absentmindedness, or automatism — they keep strictly to one path and continually recur to one idea despite interruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A common comic type is 'a character following up his one idea' (Moliere): the transition from refusing to hear, to refusing to see, to seeing only what one wants; this rigidity leads to the characteristic comic illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of comic logic to dream logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic illusion is akin to dream illusion: the mind uses perception to embody favored recollections rather than using recollections to interpret perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dream mechanisms (partial sensory input, privileged recollection, relaxed reasoning) recur in comic scenes; thus many comic effects resemble dreams in structure and feel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relaxation of rules of reasoning / abridged reasonings
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic reasonings are recognizably false but resemble the slack, abridged reasoning of a mind half-asleep; sometimes only beginning and end of an argument are given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lack of intellectual tension provides relief from effort and breeds many 'witticisms'; as relations between ideas become superficial, the play drifts toward wordplay and sound over meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play upon words arising from superficial idea-relations
rubrics_metrics.description: As idea-relations become more superficial the comic play tends toward pun, sound-based nonsense and repetition of distorted sounds detached from meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to falling asleep while people talk: sounds lose meaning and recombine to form strange meanings; stage examples where one character repeats nonsensically another's whispers (e.g., Petit-Jean and The Prompter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic obsessions and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of the same image, phrase, or burden across different contexts produces a comic effect resembling the recurrence of images in successive dreams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A musical 'burden' recurring unchanged at the end of verses with different meanings, or repeated images in fiction/stage, create a dreamlike, comic obsession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive crescendo toward absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of gradual concessions of reason that compound until the culminating absurdity is reached, producing a growing, exhilarating sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This crescendo mirrors certain tipsy or dreamy states and is used in plays (e.g., Moliere's Monsieur de Pourceaugnac, Bourgeois gentilhomme) to lull the audience into an extravagant dream and then rouse them when the play ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fusion or confusion of identities (dreamlike doubling)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dream-like blending where persons fuse yet remain distinct (one is both self and other), producing comic confusion in scenes where speaker and subject overlap ambiguously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include dialogues where a narrator is also a participant but speaks as if a third person (Mark Twain's twin anecdote); such identity slippage, common in dreams, yields comic effect distinct from mere mistaken identity (e.g., Amphitryon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial sympathetic relaxation (invitation to play)
rubrics_metrics.description: The laugher's first reaction is brief sympathy: we momentarily adopt the comic character's place, gestures, and actions and join the 'game,' experiencing relaxation from intellectual tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fleeting sympathy reduces strain of thinking and invites us to 'take it easy' with the comic character; but the sympathy is short-lived and often precedes judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as corrective/humiliatory social function
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter primarily serves to humiliate and correct those who take liberties with society; it is a social retaliation to enforce conformity rather than an act of benevolence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although laughter can produce useful correction and improvement, it is fundamentally punitive and must make a painful impression on its object to be effective; it often lacks individual justice because it operates spontaneously, not by reflective deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanistic, spontaneous nature of laughter (limits of justice and kindness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is a spontaneous mechanism set up by nature or social habit; it goes off instantly and cannot always discriminate, striking some innocent and sparing some guilty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because laughter is reflexive and retaliatory, it cannot be absolutely just or kindly; it aims at general results and lacks the time for careful, individual reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mischief/spite and egoism in the laugher
rubrics_metrics.description: Embedded in laughter is a spark of spite or mischief and an egoistic pleasure: the laugher pulls the laughed-at as if a marionette and may feel more self-assertive after laughing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This unpleasant element (curious pessimism, conceit) is natural and serves the social corrective function, though it is not flattering to human character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social function: laughter exposes surface disturbances while deeper social peace remains
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter highlights transient, surface-level undulations or disturbances in social life (like froth on waves) and thereby serves a useful function of calling attention to deviations from adaptability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As society improves its plastic adaptability, small disturbances are emphasized by laughter; though the effect is ephemeral and 'saline' (bitter aftertaste), it helps maintain social equilibrium by signalling and shaming deviations.
